stories.headline: Trump rally crowd chants 'deport' as president rips Ilhan Omar after federal raid
stories.note: At a packed Youngstown, Ohio, rally hours after federal agents searched Ilhan Omar's home, Trump hammered the Minnesota Democrat and the crowd answered with chants of "deport."
body: President Trump went after Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., at a Monday night campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio, just hours after federal agents carried out a search warrant at her home in the Washington, D.C., area.

Trump mocked Omar for lecturing Americans about her constitutional rights, calling her "a disaster," and widened his criticism to Minnesota's Somali community. He pointed to a shooting at a Minnesota high school homecoming event last week and to the FBI's arrest of a Somali immigrant accused of plotting an ISIS-style attack on the Mall of America. As he said "we don't want this," the crowd broke into chants of "deport."

According to two sources close to the case who spoke with Fox News Digital, the search grew out of a criminal fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father. A DOJ spokesperson confirmed that Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized warrant as part of an ongoing federal probe, and the department later said the investigation is criminal.
Omar posted on X that she was okay and called the search "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," adding that she will not be silenced.

Why it matters: Omar is one of the most polarizing figures in the Democratic Party, and a criminal probe into her immigration records gives Republicans a powerful issue on the trail weeks before the midterms, while forcing Democrats to defend her.

stories.headline: Media narrative predicting blue wave in key battleground state not meshing with local Republicans: 'Fired up'
stories.note: Iowa Republicans on the ground say the "blue wave" talk doesn't match what they're hearing at voters' doors, and that GOP voters are fired up heading into November.
body: Fox News Digital visited a Scott County Republican Party gathering in Davenport, Iowa, in early October, where local conservatives watched the first governor's debate and talked about whether the media's "blue wave" prediction for the state holds up.

Greg Guy, the GOP candidate for Scott County treasurer, said voters are worried about gas prices but see the spike as temporary once the Iran war winds down. Knocking on doors, he said, he rarely meets hostile voters and doesn't see Democrats excited to vote. State Senate candidate Cynthia Mensendick said she isn't seeing a blue wave either, and that Republicans' big worry is Iowa turning into Illinois if Democrat Rob Sand wins the governor's race.

Trump carried Iowa by about 13 points in 2024 and Republicans hold the governor's office and both legislative chambers. Scott County, which Trump won 51% to 47%, mixes urban Democrats, suburban swing voters and rural conservatives, making it a key test. The article notes that polling shows Democrats gaining momentum in the state's governor, Senate and House races, and that the party in power usually faces midterm headwinds.

Scott County GOP Vice Chair Kurt Whalen said Republicans will "ultimately come home" and that "people are still fired up for the Republican cause." Twenty-two-year-old state House candidate Dillon Fillion pointed to the 2025 tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill as the contrast with Democrats.
Why it matters: Iowa is one of the most important battlegrounds this cycle, and enthusiasm from local Republicans suggests the GOP's strength there may hold up better than national coverage predicts.

stories.headline: ATF suspends federal registration and approval rules for certain firearms
stories.note: A big win for gun owners: the ATF says it will no longer require federal registration or advance approval for silencers, short-barreled rifles and shotguns, following Trump's tax cut and a court ruling.
body: The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives announced Friday that gun owners no longer need to federally register, or get advance approval, to make or transfer silencers, short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns and items classified as "Any Other Weapons."

The change traces back to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut the National Firearms Act's manufacturing and transfer taxes on those items to $0. In August a federal judge in Texas ruled that with the tax gone, the NFA's registration and transfer requirements could no longer be justified under Congress's taxing power. The Justice Department then extended its nonenforcement policy nationwide.

ATF Director Robert Cekada said the agency is following the lead of "the President, Congress, and the courts" while staying focused on violent crime. NRA executive director John Commerford called it a historic milestone and said the administration will stop treating law-abiding Americans as if they need special permission.

Some rules still apply. Background checks and record-keeping under the Gun Control Act remain in place, machine guns and destructive devices are still covered by the NFA, and moving short-barreled rifles and shotguns across state lines still requires federal approval. The ATF will accept voluntary registrations and warned that future legal changes could bring back the old rules without automatic grandfathering.
Why it matters: It's a concrete Second Amendment win that Republicans can point to as a direct result of their 2025 tax law, delivered just weeks before the midterms.

stories.headline: DNC Chair Ken Martin defends 'Big Tent' strategy when pressed on democratic socialists
stories.note: DNC Chair Ken Martin wouldn't distance his party from the Democratic Socialists of America, handing Republicans fresh ammunition to tie Democrats to the far left.
body: Pressed on MSNOW about whether the Democratic Socialists of America are a liability for Democrats heading into the midterms, DNC Chairman Ken Martin defended his "big tent" approach instead of putting distance between the party and the group.

Martin said parties win "through addition, not subtraction" and that Democrats must keep growing their coalition. When anchor Peter Alexander asked whether there was a middle ground, Martin said no, arguing most Americans sit near the center but that the party can still bring in new voices.

The Republican National Committee quickly responded on X, saying Martin "embraces far-Left radicals who want to abolish the police, prisons, and borders." The DSA has pushed policies including abolishing police, prisons and ICE and expanding public ownership.

Earlier this month, the White House Council of Economic Advisers estimated that seven major DSA policies would add $49 trillion to deficits over 10 years, more than $350,000 per household. Many mainstream Democrats have tried to separate themselves from the DSA label by stressing their support for capitalism.
Why it matters: Republicans are making the DSA a central midterm attack, and the head of the Democratic Party declining to draw a line makes that message easier to land with swing voters.

stories.headline: Mamdani unveils sweeping NYPD use-of-force review, but stops short of fulfilling key campaign promises
stories.note: Nine months in, NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's new NYPD review still leaves key promises unkept, and public urination summonses have actually gone up under him.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced an internal review of the NYPD's use of force on Monday, along with an extra $2.6 million for the department's Office of Inspector General and a new rule to notify state authorities when officers facing discipline retire, so the state can consider decertifying them.

The review follows the May 2026 retirement, before any disciplinary trial, of one of the officers involved in the 2024 shooting of 19-year-old Win Rozario during a mental health crisis. Attorney General Letitia James' office declined to file criminal charges in December 2025.

But the plan falls short of several pledges Mamdani made on the campaign trail. He promised to disband the Strategic Response Group, a unit known for aggressive protest tactics, to scrap the NYPD's gang database, and to move police away from low-level offenses like public urination and open containers. All of those remain in place, and public urination summonses have climbed 18% on his watch, according to recent reporting.

Mamdani also kept Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, who was appointed by his predecessor, Eric Adams. His office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's questions about whether his police plans have changed.

Why it matters: Mamdani is the face of the Democrats' socialist wing, and the gap between his campaign promises and his record gives Republicans an easy example of far-left governing that doesn't deliver.

stories.headline: Booker ‘wowed’ by GOP challenger’s blunt message to Trump
stories.note: Cory Booker's Republican challenger Justin Murphy drew loud applause at their New Jersey Senate debate with a blunt message for Trump on Iran: "Finish it."
body: At Thursday's New Jersey Senate debate, Republican challenger Justin Murphy, a Pine Barrens attorney and former Tabernacle deputy mayor, was asked what he'd tell President Trump if he called for advice on the war in Iran. His answer, to finish the war the right way, drew loud applause.

Murphy called Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps a radical terrorist group that has robbed the Iranian people of a decent life, and said the U.S. can't quit halfway. He capped it by telling Trump to "put your cowboy hat on" and get the job done.

Booker visibly mouthed "Wow" and then called it the kind of "Yahoo" foreign policy that has dragged the U.S. into war after war in the Middle East. He also took shots at Trump, saying he "bankrupted our casinos" and ignores his advisers.

Murphy also got attention for raising illegal immigration, describing a home near a campaign stop where a child was allegedly abducted and raped by a Guatemalan illegal immigrant whom the Biden administration had earlier released, according to WRNJ.

Why it matters: New Jersey hasn't elected a Republican senator since 1972, but the state has trended redder and Trump flipped key areas in 2024. A viral debate moment puts Murphy on the map in a race Democrats have long taken for granted.
